status_reason: Provisional: both streams and the target variables (protein, fat) are stated, but install points, stream conditions and concentration ranges are not, so no client answers are yet available.
answer: Test NIR first, with a transmission/transflection probe on the whey stream and a flush-mounted reflection probe on the milk concentrate, each with its own calibration. A single shared interface is a hypothesis to test, since transmission fails on the thick, fat-rich concentrate while reflection can be less representative for clear whey. Compare this two-interface plan against a single reflection probe on the whey stream, using paired laboratory protein and fat results.

inline.headline: Test NIR on both streams with a separate interface for each: transmission/transflection for the whey, reflection for the concentrate
inline.probe: Transmission/transflection probe with a controlled 1-10 mm path for the whey; flush-mounted NIR reflection probe for the concentrate
inline.install: Whey stream and milk concentrate line, each at its own sampling point (exact points to be confirmed)
inline.fiber: Vis-NIR silica fiber (350-2400 nm, low-OH), 100-300 m cables if remote
inline.test_against: NIR diffuse reflection probe on the whey stream
inline.not_final_because: Two interfaces are a hypothesis to test; NIR needs chemometric calibration; the NIR range runs to 2500 nm but the silica fiber transmits only to 2400 nm, so the top of the range must be checked; reflection readings are sensitive to surface and fat globule size.

problems.text: The whey and the concentrate behave differently optically: the clear whey suits transmission or transflection, the opaque concentrate suits reflection. Plan a separate interface decision and a separate calibration per stream; one shared interface is a hypothesis to test.
Transmission will not work on the concentrate: when the milk is too thick or fat-rich, the light cannot penetrate the sample.
A single reflection probe is not a safe assumption for the whey: reflection can be less representative for clear liquids.
NIR is quoted to 2500 nm, but the silica fiber transmits only to 2400 nm. Confirm the spectrometer and fiber range before the pilot.

methods.why: The most common online fiber-probe method; transmission suits the whey and reflection suits the concentrate, and dairy NIR is used for fat and protein with scatter correction before PLS.
Gives well-defined peaks and molecular specificity, but MIR is limited to very thin layers and ATR probes are of high cost; use only if NIR cannot separate the classes.
Adds information complementary to NIR, but the signal is weak and can be masked by fluorescence, and it needs special probes.
Its strongly overlapping signals complicate the analysis of real mixtures, and its selectivity is low.

questions.q: Where exactly will the probes sit on each stream (pipe or vat, flow, temperature)?
questions.why: Reflection probes must be flush-mounted in the pipe or vat, and transmission path length must be controlled.

questions.q: Is the whey transparent enough at the install point for a 1-10 mm path?
questions.why: Transmission and transflection fail when the product is too thick or fat-rich.

questions.q: What protein and fat ranges occur in each stream, and how many paired laboratory samples are available?
questions.why: Calibrations for fat and protein need paired reference results across the production range.

questions.q: How far is each sampling point from the spectrometer?
questions.why: Silica fibers of 100-300 m are available, which decides between remote probes and a local analyser.

questions.q: What accuracy and sampling frequency does the pilot need for protein and fat?
questions.why: These set the go/no-go criteria for comparing the interfaces.

experiment.objective: Compare a transmission/transflection NIR probe on the whey with a reflection NIR probe on the concentrate, against laboratory protein and fat results, and test a single reflection probe on the whey as the alternative.
steps: Collect paired samples from both streams across the production range, with laboratory protein and fat analyses as reference.
Measure the whey in transmission/transflection and the concentrate in reflection with the same NIR spectrometer, building a separate calibration for each stream.
Apply MSC or SNV scatter correction before PLS for fat and protein on the concentrate.
Measure the whey with a diffuse reflection probe on the same samples, and compare with the transmission result on the same validation set.
Check that the fiber and spectrometer cover the measured range before any spectra are taken.
references: S01 p.17-18: dairy NIR reflection and transmission
S01 p.18: keeping both techniques lets models be calibrated for each stage
experiment.go_no_go: Criteria come from the client (target accuracy for protein and fat against laboratory results); not set here.

pathway.key_features: No spectra supplied yet; the key NIR features for fat and protein are to be identified by multivariate analysis in the lab trial.
pathway.path_reason: Lab trials on the two streams come first, then a chemometric model (Path A) once key features are found.

multispectral.why: Raman adds non-polar molecular information that NIR may miss, but dairy sources give no composition gain for this pair; the fusion gain shown is from a pharmaceutical study.
multispectral.test: After the single-method NIR result, compare NIR alone with NIR + Raman on the same validation set; combine only if the combination beats NIR alone.
